s: the Trojan War is recounted the series of the war
q: At length, as fate and her ill stars requir’d, To hear the series of the war desir’d.

s: the Trojan War involves the Greeks (as combatants)
q: “Relate at large, my godlike guest,” she said, “The Grecian stratagems, the town betray’d:

s: the Trojan War includes Troy (city betrayed by stratagem)
q: “Relate at large, my godlike guest,” she said, “The Grecian stratagems, the town betray’d:

s: Aeneas's flight and wanderings follow the Trojan War (after the war)
q: The fatal issue of so long a war, Your flight, your wand’rings, and your woes, declare;

s: Aeneas's flight and wanderings occurs at ev’ry sea, ev’ry coast
q: For, since on ev’ry sea, on ev’ry coast, Your men have been distress’d, your navy toss’d,

s: Aeneas's flight and wanderings last seven years (as measured by the sun’s tropical passages)
q: For, since on ev’ry sea, on ev’ry coast, Your men have been distress’d, your navy toss’d, Sev’n times the sun has either tropic view’d,

s: Cupid is the child of Cupid's mother
q: But he, not mindless of his mother’s pray’r,

s: Jupiter is invoked at the feast (as hospitable deity)
q: “O hospitable Jove! we thus invoke, With solemn rites, thy sacred name and pow’r;

s: Juno is invoked at the feast (as gracious goddess)
q: And gracious Juno, both be present here!

s: Memnon is related to the Trojan War (his arms and troops are discussed)
q: Then ask’d what arms the swarthy Memnon wore, What troops he landed on the Trojan shore;

s: Diomede is related to the Trojan War (his steeds are discussed)
q: The steeds of Diomede varied the discourse,

s: Cupid causes love in Dido (by divine influence)
q: But he, not mindless of his mother’s pray’r, Works in the pliant bosom of the fair, And moulds her heart anew, and blots her former care.

s: Achilles is related to the Trojan War (his force is discussed)
q: And fierce Achilles, with his matchless force;

s: Dido is a queen (royal dame of Tyre)
q: But, far above the rest, the royal dame, (Already doom’d to love’s disastrous flame,)

s: Dido loves Aeneas (after Cupid removes her former care)
q: The dead is to the living love resign’d; And all Aeneas enters in her mind.

s: Dido has former love the dead beloved (Dido's former love) (deceased)
q: The dead is to the living love resign’d;

s: Dido hosts Aeneas (as her princely guest)
q: The queen already sate Amidst the Trojan lords, in shining state, High on a golden bed: her princely guest Was next her side;

s: Dido presides over the feast (as queen)
q: The queen already sate Amidst the Trojan lords, in shining state,

s: Aeneas is a Trojan (narrator of Troy’s destruction)
q: All were attentive to the godlike man, When from his lofty couch he thus began: “Great queen, what you command me to relate Renews the sad remembrance of our fate: An empire from its old foundations rent, And ev’ry woe the Trojans underwent; A peopled city made a desert place; All that I saw, and part of which I was:

s: the Trojan horse is made of pine planks (with hollow sides)
q: The sides were plank’d with pine; they feign’d it made For their return, and this the vow they paid.

s: the Trojan horse contains Greek soldiers (hidden inside)
q: Thus they pretend, but in the hollow side Selected numbers of their soldiers hide: With inward arms the dire machine they load, And iron bowels stuff the dark abode.

s: the Trojan horse is built by Epeus (the maker of the fatal engine)
q: Nor injur’d Menelaus, nor the fam’d Epeus, who the fatal engine fram’d.

s: the Trojan horse is intended as the fatal present (hidden frauds)
q: But Capys, and the rest of sounder mind, The fatal present to the flames designed, Or to the wat’ry deep; at least to bore The hollow sides, and hidden frauds explore.

s: Sinon is a Greek captive (bound and unarmed before Priam)
q: Meantime, with shouts, the Trojan shepherds bring A captive Greek, in bands, before the king;

s: Sinon is from Greece (by his own account)
q: Greece is my country, Sinon is my name.

s: Sinon opens the Trojan horse (at night)
q: When Sinon, favour’d by the partial gods, Unlock’d the horse, and op’d his dark abodes; Restor’d to vital air our hidden foes, Who joyful from their long confinement rose.

s: Laocoon is a priest (Neptune’s priest)
q: Laocoon, Neptune’s priest by lot that year, With solemn pomp then sacrific’d a steer;

s: Laocoon warns against the Trojan horse (publicly and emphatically)
q: ‘O wretched countrymen! what fury reigns? What more than madness has possess’d your brains? Think you the Grecians from your coasts are gone? And are Ulysses’ arts no better known? This hollow fabric either must inclose, Within its blind recess, our secret foes; Or ’tis an engine rais’d above the town, T’ o’erlook the walls, and then to batter down. Somewhat is sure design’d, by fraud or force: Trust not their presents, nor admit the horse.’

s: Troy is a city (Trojan city)
q: An empire from its old foundations rent, And ev’ry woe the Trojans underwent; A peopled city made a desert place;

s: Laocoon is attacked by their winding volumes (Twice round his waist and twice about his gasping throat)
q: The wretched father, running to their aid With pious haste, but vain, they next invade; Twice round his waist their winding volumes roll’d; And twice about his gasping throat they fold.

s: Laocoon’s children are killed by the two serpents (before Laocoon is attacked)
q: And to Laocoon and his children make; And first around the tender boys they wind, Then with their sharpen’d fangs their limbs and bodies grind.

s: the two serpents come from the sea (as a terrifying portent)
q: When, dreadful to behold, from sea we spied Two serpents, rank’d abreast, the seas divide, And smoothly sweep along the swelling tide.

s: the two serpents protect Minerva (by resting at her tower)
q: Their tasks perform’d, the serpents quit their prey, And to the tow’r of Pallas make their way: Couch’d at her feet, they lie protected there By her large buckler and protended spear.

s: Minerva provides aid (the Grecian hopes, and all th’ attempts they made)
q: The Grecian hopes, and all th’ attempts they made, Were only founded on Minerva’s aid.

s: Minerva has her fatal image (drawn from the temple)
q: But from the time when impious Diomede, And false Ulysses, that inventive head, Her fatal image from the temple drew,

s: Ulysses takes advantage of their fright
q: Ulysses took th’ advantage of their fright; Call’d Calchas, and produc’d in open sight:

s: Ulysses frames Sinon’s false accusation (against Palamedes)
q: But when Ulysses, with fallacious arts, Had made impression in the people’s hearts, And forg’d a treason in my patron’s name

s: Diomede steals the Palladium (with Ulysses)
q: But from the time when impious Diomede, And false Ulysses, that inventive head, Her fatal image from the temple drew,

s: Troy has walls the Trojan walls
q: But if it climb, with your assisting hands, The Trojan walls, and in the city stands; Then Troy shall Argos and Mycenae burn,

s: Calchas pronounces Sinon
q: But, as it was agreed, pronounc’d that I Was destin’d by the wrathful gods to die.

s: Tenedos is a island (located in sight of Troy)
q: In sight of Troy lies Tenedos, an isle

s: the Greek fleet is concealed at There (we thought their sails were hoisted for Greece)
q: There was their fleet conceal’d. We thought, for Greece Their sails were hoisted, and our fears release.

s: the Greeks’ escape from Troy is thought to have departed for Greece (their sails were hoisted)
q: We thought, for Greece Their sails were hoisted, and our fears release.

s: Fate determines the fall of Troy (with divine design)
q: And, had not Heav’n the fall of Troy design’d, Or had not men been fated to be blind, Enough was said and done t’inspire a better mind.

s: the gods determine the fall of Troy (through fate and omens)
q: And, had not Heav’n the fall of Troy design’d, Or had not men been fated to be blind, Enough was said and done t’inspire a better mind.

s: the sack of Troy is enabled by False tears and fawning words
q: What Diomede, nor Thetis’ greater son, A thousand ships, nor ten years’ siege, had done: False tears and fawning words the city won.

s: Troy is destined to fall the flames (according to Sinon’s deceptive prophecy)
q: For, once admitted there, our hopes are lost; And Troy may then a new Palladium boast; For so religion and the gods ordain, That, if you violate with hands profane Minerva’s gift, your town in flames shall burn,

s: the Trojans are confined within Troy (during the siege)
q: The Trojans, coop’d within their walls so long, Unbar their gates, and issue in a throng,

s: the Greeks are weary of Trojan War (after prolonged warfare)
q: By destiny compell’d, and in despair, The Greeks grew weary of the tedious war,

s: the Trojan War lasts ten years (before Troy’s capture)
q: BOOK II THE ARGUMENT. Aeneas relates how the city of Troy was taken, after a ten years’ siege,

s: Trojan War lasts ten years (of Troy)
q: Aeneas relates how the city of Troy was taken, after a ten years’ siege, by the treachery of Sinon, and the stratagem of a wooden horse.

s: the Trojan horse is a fabric (constructed in the shape of a monstrous steed)
q: And by Minerva’s aid a fabric rear’d, Which like a steed of monstrous height appear’d:

s: Hector returns from toils Of war (triumphant)
q: Unlike that Hector who return’d from toils Of war, triumphant, in Aeacian spoils,

s: Priam rules Asia (as its monarch)
q: He, who the scepter of all Asia sway’d, Whom monarchs like domestic slaves obey’d.

s: Priam is father of Polites
q: Behold! Polites, one of Priam’s sons,

s: Hecuba seeks shelter Priam (with all her helpless train Of dames)
q: Here Hecuba, with all her helpless train Of dames, for shelter sought, but sought in vain.

s: Cassandra is a prophetess (royal Trojan)
q: Behold the royal prophetess, the fair Cassandra, dragg’d by her dishevel’d hair,

s: Cassandra is loved by Coroebus (as the woman he sought to marry)
q: With young Coroebus, who by love was led To win renown and fair Cassandra’s bed,

s: Cassandra is protected by Minerva’s shrine (but not successfully)
q: Whom not Minerva’s shrine, nor sacred bands, In safety could protect from sacrilegious hands:

s: Coroebus leads Trojan troops (brought to Priam’s aid)
q: And lately brought his troops to Priam’s aid, Forewarn’d in vain by the prophetic maid.

s: Coroebus is killed by Peneleus (at Pallas’ altar)
q: Coroebus first, At Pallas’ altar, by Peneleus pierc’d.

s: Pantheus is a priest of Apollo (who escaped the Greek attack)
q: Pantheus, Apollo’s priest, a sacred name, Had scap’d the Grecian swords, and pass’d the flame:

s: Hector is killed by Achilles (in the Trojan war)
q: Such as he was, when, by Pelides slain, Thessalian coursers dragg’d him o’er the plain.

s: Pyrrhus stands at the gate (threat’ning loud, With glitt’ring arms)
q: Before the gate stood Pyrrhus, threat’ning loud, With glitt’ring arms conspicuous in the crowd.

s: household gods accompany Aeneas (in exile and future settlement)
q: Now Troy to thee commends her future state, And gives her gods companions of thy fate:

s: the Greeks possess the wall (already)
q: The foes already have possess’d the wall; Troy nods from high, and totters to her fall.

s: the Greeks emerges from the fatal horse (armed hosts, an unexpected force)
q: And armed hosts, an unexpected force, Break from the bowels of the fatal horse.

s: the Trojans defend Troy (desperately and unsuccessfully)
q: Then let us fall, but fall amidst our foes: Despair of life the means of living shows.’

s: Troy is a city (ancient and imperial)
q: What tongue can tell the slaughter of that night? What eyes can weep the sorrows and affright? An ancient and imperial city falls:

s: Troy is consumed by The fire (the foe commands)
q: The fire consumes the town, the foe commands;

s: Hector defends Troy (as its champion)
q: O light of Trojans, and support of Troy, Thy father’s champion, and thy country’s joy!

s: Troy totters to her fall
q: Troy nods from high, and totters to her fall.

s: Ilium is a town (no longer existing after its destruction)
q: ‘Troy is no more, and Ilium was a town!

s: the Trojan palace is the palace of Deiphobus (ascends In smoky flames)
q: The palace of Deiphobus ascends In smoky flames, and catches on his friends.

s: the Trojan palace contains Priam (before its capture)
q: New clamours from th’ invested palace ring: We run to die, or disengage the king.

s: the Trojan horse contains the Greeks (concealed within its hollow body)
q: And armed hosts, an unexpected force, Break from the bowels of the fatal horse.

s: the fall of Troy is caused by Fate (as an irrevocable decree)
q: When wrathful Jove’s irrevocable doom Transfers the Trojan state to Grecian hands.

s: Fate transfers Troy (to Greek rule)
q: When wrathful Jove’s irrevocable doom Transfers the Trojan state to Grecian hands.

s: the slaughter of the night occurs in that night
q: What tongue can tell the slaughter of that night? What eyes can weep the sorrows and affright? An ancient and imperial city falls:

s: the sack of Troy includes the fall of Priam (with Troy in ashes)
q: Thus Priam fell, and shar’d one common fate With Troy in ashes, and his ruin’d state:

s: Hector appears as a bloody ghost (to Aeneas in a vision)
q: When Hector’s ghost before my sight appears: A bloody shroud he seem’d, and bath’d in tears;

s: Hector has wounds (suffered for his country and now streaming afresh)
q: And all the wounds he for his country bore Now stream’d afresh, and with new purple ran.

s: Aeneas is a goddess-born hero
q: ‘O goddess-born! escape, by timely flight, The flames and horrors of this fatal night.

s: Aeneas receives household gods (as companions of his fate)
q: Now Troy to thee commends her future state, And gives her gods companions of thy fate:

s: Aeneas carries the statues of the gods (from their sacred abodes)
q: He said, and brought me, from their blest abodes, The venerable statues of the gods,

s: Aeneas is destined to erect walls (after long wandering)
q: From their assistance walls expect, Which, wand’ring long, at last thou shalt erect.’

s: Aeneas is a the Trojan exile
q: Thus having pass’d the night in fruitless pain, I to my longing friends return again, Amaz’d th’ augmented number to behold, Of men and matrons mix’d, of young and old; A wretched exil’d crew together brought, With arms appointed, and with treasure fraught, Resolv’d, and willing, under my command, To run all hazards both of sea and land.

s: Anchises has wife my celestial wife (loath’d by the gods)
q: ’Tis long since I, for my celestial wife Loath’d by the gods, have dragg’d a ling’ring life;

s: Anchises initially refuses the sack of Troy (resolved to die in Troy)
q: The good Anchises, whom, by timely flight, I purpos’d to secure on Ida’s height, Refus’d the journey, resolute to die And add his fun’rals to the fate of Troy,

s: Anchises is versed in omens
q: But old Anchises, vers’d in omens, rear’d His hands to heav’n, and this request preferr’d:

s: Creusa is wife of Aeneas (forsaken during the escape)
q: Again I thought on my forsaken wife, And trembled for my son’s abandon’d life.

s: Creusa has son your son’s
q: Take us along to share your destiny. If any farther hopes in arms remain, This place, these pledges of your love, maintain. To whom do you expose your father’s life, Your son’s, and mine, your now forgotten wife!’

s: Creusa is lost in the sack of Troy (never to be recovered alive)
q: Alas! I lost Creusa: hard to tell If by her fatal destiny she fell, Or weary sate, or wander’d with affright; But she was lost for ever to my sight.

s: Creusa becomes Creusa’s death (her ghost appears after death)
q: Appears, no more Creusa, nor my wife, But a pale spectre, larger than the life.

s: Creusa is destined to remain in Troy (by divine fate)
q: My fates permit me not from hence to fly; Nor he, the great controller of the sky.

s: Ascanius is a child (Aeneas’s son)
q: My hand shall lead our little son; and you, My faithful consort, shall our steps pursue.

s: Ascanius is protected by Aeneas (during the flight from Troy)
q: My hand shall lead our little son; and you, My faithful consort, shall our steps pursue.

s: Aeneas is son of Anchises
q: Haste, my dear father, (’tis no time to wait,) And load my shoulders with a willing freight.

s: Ascanius is marked by the omens concerning Ascanius (sacred flame and heavenly sign)
q: Strange to relate, from young Iulus’ head A lambent flame arose, which gently spread Around his brows, and on his temples fed.

s: Venus is a goddess (Aeneas’s mother)
q: My mother stood reveal’d before my sight Never so radiant did her eyes appear; Not her own star confess’d a light so clear: Great in her charms, as when on gods above She looks, and breathes herself into their love.

s: Venus protects Aeneas (from the destruction of Troy)
q: And these had perish’d in the nightly war, But for my presence and protecting care.

s: Helen is a common bane of Greece and Troy
q: But, by the flames that cast their blaze around, That common bane of Greece and Troy I found.

s: Helen is fearful of vengeance (because Troy is burning)
q: For Ilium burnt, she dreads the Trojan sword; More dreads the vengeance of her injur’d lord;

s: Troy is destroyed by the gods
q: Not Helen’s face, nor Paris, was in fault; But by the gods was this destruction brought.

s: Troy is destroyed by the gods
q: Not Helen’s face, nor Paris, was in fault; But by the gods was this destruction brought.

s: the destruction of Troy is caused by the gods
q: Not Helen’s face, nor Paris, was in fault; But by the gods was this destruction brought.

s: the fire of Troy is fueled by Vulcan (with rising winds)
q: With Vulcan’s rage the rising winds conspire, And near our palace roll the flood of fire.

s: Aeneas is son of Venus (divine mother)
q: My mother stood reveal’d before my sight

s: the sack of Troy is led by my command (to run all hazards both of sea and land)
q: Resolv’d, and willing, under my command, To run all hazards both of sea and land.

s: the Trojan exile is destined for Latium (after prolonged wandering)
q: Then, after many painful years are past, On Latium’s happy shore you shall be cast,

s: the Trojan exile contains A wretched exil’d crew (with arms appointed, and with treasure fraught)
q: A wretched exil’d crew together brought, With arms appointed, and with treasure fraught,

s: the Trojans are led by Aeneas (as an exiled community)
q: Resolv’d, and willing, under my command, To run all hazards both of sea and land.

s: the gods control Fate
q: You bear no more than what the gods ordain.

s: the gods destroy Troy (through divine intervention)
q: But by the gods was this destruction brought.

s: Fate determines Creusa’s death (as an unavoidable destiny)
q: My fates permit me not from hence to fly; Nor he, the great controller of the sky.

s: Fate destines Aeneas (for Latium and a future kingdom)
q: There end your toils; and there your fates provide A quiet kingdom, and a royal bride:

s: the Trojan household gods are carried by Anchises (during the flight from Troy)
q: Our country gods, the relics, and the bands, Hold you, my father, in your guiltless hands:

s: Aeneas is husband of Creusa (lawful wife)
q: Then thus the ghost began to soothe my grief ‘Nor tears, nor cries, can give the dead relief. Desist, my much-lov’d lord, t’ indulge your pain;

s: Ida is intended as a refuge for Anchises (by timely flight)
q: The good Anchises, whom, by timely flight, I purpos’d to secure on Ida’s height,

s: Latium is a future homeland (where Aeneas’s toil ends)
q: Then, after many painful years are past, On Latium’s happy shore you shall be cast, Where gentle Tiber from his bed beholds The flow’ry meadows, and the feeding folds.

s: Tiber beholds The flow’ry meadows (from his bed; and the feeding folds)
q: Where gentle Tiber from his bed beholds The flow’ry meadows, and the feeding folds.

s: Aeneas is father of Ascanius
q: Look if your helpless father yet survive, Or if Ascanius or Creusa live.

s: Aeneas is protected by Venus (during the escape from Troy)
q: And these had perish’d in the nightly war, But for my presence and protecting care.

s: Aeneas is destined for Latium (after long wanderings by land and sea)
q: Long wand’ring ways for you the pow’rs decree; On land hard labours, and a length of sea. Then, after many painful years are past, On Latium’s happy shore you shall be cast,

s: Aeneas is provided with A quiet kingdom (by your fates; and a royal bride)
q: There end your toils; and there your fates provide A quiet kingdom, and a royal bride: There fortune shall the Trojan line restore, And you for lost Creusa weep no more.

s: Anchises is intended to be secured on Ida’s height (by timely flight)
q: The good Anchises, whom, by timely flight, I purpos’d to secure on Ida’s height,

s: Aeneas is a Trojan (leader and narrator)
q: When Heav’n had overturn’d the Trojan state And Priam’s throne, by too severe a fate; When ruin’d Troy became the Grecians’ prey, And Ilium’s lofty tow’rs in ashes lay; Warn’d by celestial omens, we retreat, To seek in foreign lands a happier seat.

s: Polydore is sent to Thracia (loaded with gold)
q: Old Priam, fearful of the war’s event, This hapless Polydore to Thracia sent: Loaded with gold, he sent his darling, far From noise and tumults, and destructive war,

s: Polydore is murdered in Polydore’s murder (for his wealth by the Thracian tyrant)
q: Who, when he saw the pow’r of Troy decline, Forsook the weaker, with the strong to join; Broke ev’ry bond of nature and of truth, And murder’d, for his wealth, the royal youth.

s: Troy falls in the fall of Troy (to the Greeks)
q: When ruin’d Troy became the Grecians’ prey, And Ilium’s lofty tow’rs in ashes lay;

s: the Greeks conquer Troy (after the Trojan state is overturned)
q: When ruin’d Troy became the Grecians’ prey, And Ilium’s lofty tow’rs in ashes lay;

s: Thrace is ruled by Lycurgus (formerly)
q: Against our coast appears a spacious land, Which once the fierce Lycurgus did command, Thracia the name; the people bold in war;

s: Thrace is a hospitable realm (while Fate was kind)
q: A hospitable realm while Fate was kind, With Troy in friendship and religion join’d.

s: the ships is built at Ida (from timber of sacred groves)
q: Near old Antandros, and at Ida’s foot, The timber of the sacred groves we cut, And build our fleet; uncertain yet to find What place the gods for our repose assign’d.

s: Aeneas is son of Anchises
q: All are concern’d to know what place the god Assign’d, and where determin’d our abode. My father, long revolving in his mind The race and lineage of the Trojan kind,

s: the ships sails to Delos (after leaving Thrace)
q: Now, when the raging storms no longer reign, But southern gales invite us to the main, We launch our vessels, with a prosp’rous wind, And leave the cities and the shores behind.

s: Delos is a island (in the Aegean Sea)
q: An island in th’ Aegaean main appears; Neptune and wat’ry Doris claim it theirs.

s: Apollo’s oracle directs Aeneas (to seek the ancestors’ motherland)
q: ‘Undaunted youths, go, seek that mother earth From which your ancestors derive their birth. The soil that sent you forth, her ancient race In her old bosom shall again embrace.

s: settlement in Crete is established by Aeneas (after the mistaken oracle interpretation)
q: With eager haste a rising town I frame, Which from the Trojan Pergamus I name: The name itself was grateful; I exhort To found their houses, and erect a fort.

s: Cretan plague afflicts the Trojans (after settlement in Crete)
q: When rising vapours choke the wholesome air, And blasts of noisome winds corrupt the year; The trees devouring caterpillars burn; Parch’d was the grass, and blighted was the corn: Nor ’scape the beasts; for Sirius, from on high, With pestilential heat infects the sky: My men, some fall, the rest in fevers fry.

s: Hesperia is a fruitful land (with bold natives)
q: A land there is, Hesperia call’d of old, The soil is fruitful, and the natives bold.

s: Hesperia is ancestral home of household gods (the place from which they came and to which they must return)
q: Jasius there and Dardanus were born; From thence we came, and thither must return.

s: Aeneas leads the Trojans (in seeking a new homeland)
q: Warn’d by celestial omens, we retreat, To seek in foreign lands a happier seat.

s: Strophades is a islands (in the Ionian Sea)
q: At length I land upon the Strophades, Safe from the danger of the stormy seas. Those isles are compass’d by th’ Ionian main,

s: Strophades is home of Harpies (their dire abode)
q: Those isles are compass’d by th’ Ionian main, The dire abode where the foul Harpies reign,

s: Harpies is a monsters (winged, foul, and human-punishing)
q: Monsters more fierce offended Heav’n ne’er sent From hell’s abyss, for human punishment: With virgin faces, but with wombs obscene, Foul paunches, and with ordure still unclean; With claws for hands, and looks for ever lean.

s: Celaeno is messenger of Fate
q: Yet one remain’d, the messenger of Fate: High on a craggy cliff Celaeno sate, And thus her dismal errand did relate:

s: Celaeno is queen of the Furies (as stated in her prophecy)
q: Heed therefore what I say; and keep in mind What Jove decrees, what Phoebus has design’d, And I, the Furies’ queen, from both relate:

s: Celaeno pronounces the Harpies’ curse (against the Trojans)
q: But know, that ere your promis’d walls you build, My curses shall severely be fulfill’d. Fierce famine is your lot for this misdeed, Reduc’d to grind the plates on which you feed.’

s: the Harpies’ curse foretells famine (before the Trojans build their promised walls)
q: Fierce famine is your lot for this misdeed, Reduc’d to grind the plates on which you feed.’

s: Helenus is a seer (royal and prophetic)
q: Then to the royal seer I thus began: ‘O thou, who know’st, beyond the reach of man, The laws of heav’n, and what the stars decree;

s: Helenus reigns in Greece (succeeded Pyrrhus in his bed and throne)
q: How Helenus reviv’d the Trojan name, And reign’d in Greece; that Priam’s captive son Succeeded Pyrrhus in his bed and throne;

s: Helenus is husband of Andromache (after Pyrrhus relinquishes her)
q: Then me to Trojan Helenus resign’d, And his two slaves in equal marriage join’d;

s: Aeneas builds the ships (near Antandros and at Ida’s foot)
q: Near old Antandros, and at Ida’s foot, The timber of the sacred groves we cut, And build our fleet; uncertain yet to find What place the gods for our repose assign’d.

s: Andromache is given to Helenus (by Pyrrhus after he seeks Helen)
q: Cloy’d with possession, he forsook my bed, And Helen’s lovely daughter sought to wed; Then me to Trojan Helenus resign’d,

s: Hector is husband of Andromache (before the fall of Troy)
q: What have you suffer’d since you lost your lord? By what strange blessing are you now restor’d? Still are you Hector’s? or is Hector fled,

s: Aeneas names Aenos (after himself)
